aboutAuthor: Michael Mauboussin is Head of Consilient Research at Counterpoint Global and a leading thinker on valuation and decision-making. Alfred Rappaport pioneered shareholder value analysis. Together they translate DCF theory into a practical lens for testing what the market already believes.

points.heading: Price is a mirror of expectations
points.body: Every quote embeds assumptions about growth, margin, and duration. Reverse-engineer those price-implied expectations first, then test the story against fundamentals rather than forecasting earnings in a vacuum.

points.heading: Value lives in duration of advantage
points.body: How long ROIC stays above WACC explains more of value than next quarter's EPS. Fade curves by industry, from airlines to software, translate strategic moats into numerical horizons price must imply.

points.heading: Extrapolation is the most expensive bias
points.body: Trends feel permanent, so prices embed trend extension. From homebuilders in 2005 to growth darlings, the gap between implied share or margin and base rates flags fantasy before it reprices.

points.heading: Triangulate with options and multiples
points.body: A vanilla DCF misses optionality in biotech and network inflections in platforms. Cross-check with real options and EV-to-capital versus ROIC scatters so no hidden expectation goes unexamined.

points.heading: Corporate actions arbitrage expectations
points.body: M&A premia, buybacks, and guidance are not just signals; they trade one set of expectations for another. Buying stock creates value only when the expectations you retire are conservative.

points.heading: Opportunity needs a revision catalyst
points.body: A gap without a reason to close is just a cheap story. Map informational, behavioral, strategic, and organizational sources of gaps to catalysts like earnings, investor days, or refund cycles and size accordingly.

insights: Coca-Cola's late-1990s price demanded impossible double-digit growth for decades, proving great companies can be terrible investments at the wrong price.
Dell's negative cash conversion cycle shows investment efficiency can create more value than faster revenue growth.
The horse-race of low-PIE versus high-PIE stocks demonstrates that humility about mean reversion systematically wins.
conclusion: Expectations Investing teaches a diagnostic habit: read the story price tells, compare it to the economics strategy can actually deliver, and act only where a plausible revision awaits. The market rewards those who listen to price before trying to outguess it.
